questions.question: A cache uses hash(key) % 4 to pick one of four servers. You add a fifth server. Roughly what fraction of keys now map to a different server?
options: About 20% — only the new server's share moves
About 80% — the divisor changed, so most keys move
About 25% — one server's worth
None — hashing is stable by definition
questions.explanation: Changing the divisor from 4 to 5 changes the result for any key where hash%4 and hash%5 disagree, which is most of them. Measured on 10,000 keys: 81%. Every one of those is a cache miss hitting the database, at the moment you were already under enough load to need a fifth server.

questions.question: What is the primary guarantee consistent hashing provides?
options: Keys are distributed perfectly evenly across nodes
Lookups become O(1) instead of O(log n)
The number of keys that move when the node set changes is bounded to roughly 1/N
Hash collisions become impossible
questions.explanation: The guarantee is about stability under topology change, not evenness. A ring with one virtual node per physical node already has good churn but terrible balance (measured spread: 540x). Even distribution is a separate property that virtual nodes provide.

questions.question: In a ring, a key is owned by the first node found walking clockwise from the key's position. What happens to a key that hashes above the highest node position on the circle?
options: It has no owner and the lookup returns an error
It wraps around to the lowest node position
It is assigned to the node with the most free capacity
It is rehashed with a different seed until it lands lower
questions.explanation: The wrap is what makes it a circle rather than a line. In code it is the `if i == len(r.slots) { i = 0 }` branch after the binary search. Omit it and every key above the top slot loses its owner.

questions.question: You measure spread (busiest node / quietest node) for 5 nodes: 1 vnode = 540, 50 vnodes = 1.60, 150 vnodes = 1.50, 500 vnodes = 1.74. What should you conclude?
options: More virtual nodes always improve balance, so use as many as memory allows
Balance improves sharply up to a plateau near 50, after which extra vnodes buy noise, not fairness
The measurement is broken, since 500 should beat 150
Virtual nodes have no effect on balance
questions.explanation: The curve plateaus. 500 scoring worse than 150 is hash noise within a flat region, not a trend. Past the plateau you pay memory and lookup time for nothing. This is why Cassandra reduced its default num_tokens from 256 to 16.

questions.question: One key on your site goes viral and receives 40% of all traffic. You increase virtual nodes from 150 to 1000. What happens to the load on the node owning that key?
options: It drops by roughly 6x as the key is spread across more positions
It drops slightly, since the arcs are now smaller
Nothing — one key hashes to one position and therefore one node
It increases, because more virtual nodes mean more lookups
questions.explanation: Virtual nodes balance the *keyspace*, not traffic per key. A single key is a single hash value with a single owner regardless of replica count. Hot keys need a different mechanism: replication of that key, request coalescing, or a local cache in front.

questions.question: Your team refactors virtualKey from node + "#" + i to fmt.Sprintf("%s-%d", node, i). Tests still pass. What have you shipped?
options: Nothing — it is an internal naming detail
A performance regression from the extra formatting
A full remap: every virtual node lands at a new position, so effectively every key changes owner
A collision risk, but existing keys stay put
questions.explanation: The virtual-node naming scheme is part of the ring's contract, because it determines every position on the circle. Change the format and the whole topology reshuffles — a total cache flush shipped as a cleanup commit. Unit tests pass because each individual mapping is still internally consistent.
